title_ar: الكلام على الصور الفوتوغرافية وأدلة جوازها
title_en: On Photographic Images and the Evidence for Their Permissibility
body_ar:
السؤال الوارد : في كتاب تفسير آيات الأحكام ترجيح جواز الصور الفوتوغرافية، وقد سمعت أنكم تجيزونها، فما هو الدليل على ذلك؟ 

الإجابة : إن الصور الفوتوغرافية ليست موجودة في العهد النبوي ولا في عهد أئمة الاجتهاد، وإنما عرفت في العصور المتأخرة.

ولذلك فالنصوص الشرعية الواردة في التصوير لا تتناولها بدلالة الألفاظ قطعاً، لأن اللفظ النبوي في التصوير إنما يتناول ما كان موجوداً إذ ذاك، فالتصوير الذي حرمه رسول الله صلى الله عليه وسلم وحذر منه هو ما كان موجوداً في زمانه وهو النحت من الحجر أو من الطين أو من الخشب أو الرسم باليد فهذا هو التصوير، وهي كذلك لا يمكن أن تقاس على الصور المحرمة، هي لا تدخل في دلالة اللفظ قطعاً، ومن فسر الألفاظ الواردة في التصوير بها فهو بمثابة من فسر نصوص القرآن بغير معانيها، كالذي يقول في قول الله تعالى: {وجاءت سيارة فأرسلوا واردهم}، أن السيارة مثلا كابرس أو لاند روفر أو نحو هذا، فهذا فسر القرآن بغير معناه.

هذا السؤال عن رأيي أنا، فلذلك تفسير هذه النصوص بغير دلالاتها اللغوية منافٍ للمقصد الشرعي وهو من القول على الله بغير علم، ولذلك فالدلالات اللغوية لو أخذ بها بتطورها وما تؤول إليه لكان قول النبي صلى الله عليه وسلم: "إن قوماً في آخر الزمان يستحلون الخمر يسمونها بغير اسمها" منافيا لهذا، لأنه لو كان تغير دلالات الألفاظ مغيراً للحكم لكان تغيير هؤلاء لاسم الخمر فيسمونها المشروب الروحي مثلاً لكان هذا مبيحاً له، لأنه قال: يسمونها بغير اسمها، ولهذا فإن من القواعد المسلمة أن تسمية الشيء بغير اسمه لا تغير حكمه، فتسمية حبس الظل تصويراً أمر ناشئ عن اصطلاحنا نحن، ولهذا لو شئنا لسميناه باسم آخر بعض الناس يسميه بالصنف، وبعضهم يسميه بالتمثيل، ولهم فيه أسماء وعبارات مختلفة، ولذلك فتسميته تصويراً لا تقتضي حرمته.

وهذه القاعدة هي التي نظمها شيخي محمد علي بن عبد الودود رحمه الله في قوله: 

تسمية العين بغير اسمها *** لا تقتضي منعاً ولا تقتضي 

بل حكمها من قبل في أمسها *** فائدة مهمة ينبغي 

لا تنقل الأعيان عن حكمها *** إثبات حق ليس في قسمها

كحكمها من بعد في يومها *** إيقاف من يفتي على فهمها

وكذلك لا يمكن أن تقاس هذه الصور الفوتوغرافية على الصور الحقيقية التي وردت فيها النصوص، لأن العلة مختلفة، فالعلة التي حرم النبي صلى الله عليه وسلم التصوير من أجلها بيّنها بأنها مضاهاة خلق الله ومحاكاته، ولذلك يعذب المصور يوم القيامة من صور ذا روح عذب حتى ينفخ فيه الروح وما هو بنافخ، ولذلك قال: "المضاهون خلقي فليخلقوا ذرة فليخلقوا شعيرة"، فلهذا بيّن علة التحريم.

وهذه العلة لا تتحقق في الصور الفوتوغرافية، ولهذا لا يمكن أن يمتدح إنسان بأنه أحسن تصويراً من غيره، لكن يمتدح بأنه أتقن وأدرى باستعمال الآلة مثلاً أو أدق في ضبطها وهذا ليس هو عين التصوير.

ومن أجل هذا فالصور الفوتوغرافية إذا كان المصور مما يحل النظر إليه يجوز عملها، ودليل ذلك أن الأصل في الأشياء كلها الإباحة وأن الحبس حبس الظل هو بمثابة النظر في المرآة، وقد ثبت أن النبي صلى الله عليه وسلم كان ينظر في المرآة. 

حكم النظر في الصور وامتلاكها

السؤال : ما حكم النظر في الصور وامتلاكها، مثلاً صورة أخ أو زوج أو صديق؟

الإجابة : إن كان ذلك بالتصوير الفوتوغرافي وليس بالتصوير الرسمي أي بالرسم فلا حرج في النظر إليه ما لم يكن فيه عورة لا يحل النظر إليها، فكل ما يجوز النظر إليه يجوز تصويره بالتصوير الفوتوغرافي.
body_en:
The question received: In the book Tafsīr Āyāt al-Aḥkām there is a preference given to the permissibility of photographic images, and I have heard that you hold them permissible. What is the evidence for that?

The answer: Photographic images did not exist in the prophetic era, nor in the era of the imams of independent legal reasoning (ijtihād); they became known only in the later ages.

For that reason, the texts of the Sharia that have come down concerning image-making (taṣwīr) do not take them in by the signification of the words, definitively — because the prophetic wording concerning image-making takes in only what existed at that time. The image-making that the Messenger of God, may God bless him and grant him peace, forbade and warned against is what existed in his time, namely carving from stone, or from clay, or from wood, or drawing by hand: that is image-making. Nor, likewise, can they be brought by analogy under the forbidden images; they do not fall under the signification of the word at all. Whoever interprets the wordings that have come down concerning image-making as covering them is in the position of one who interprets the texts of the Qur'an by other than their meanings — like the one who says, of God's saying {And there came a caravan, and they sent their water-drawer} (Sūrat Yūsuf 12:19), that the sayyārah is, say, a Caprice or a Land Rover or the like: that man has interpreted the Qur'an by other than its meaning.

This question is about my own view. So interpreting these texts by other than their linguistic significations is contrary to the purpose of the Sharia, and is speaking about God without knowledge. For if the linguistic significations were taken together with their development and with whatever they come to mean, then the saying of the Prophet, may God bless him and grant him peace — "There will be a people at the end of time who will hold wine lawful, calling it by other than its name" — would be contrary to this; because if a change in the significations of words changed the ruling, then the changing of the name of wine by those people, calling it, say, "spirits", would make it permissible for them, since he said: "calling it by other than its name". For this reason it is among the accepted maxims that naming a thing by other than its name does not change its ruling. The naming of the capturing of a shadow "image-making" is something that arises from a usage of our own; and so, had we wished, we could have named it by another name. Some people call it ṣanf, and some call it depiction (tamthīl), and they have various names and expressions for it. So calling it "image-making" does not entail that it is forbidden.

This maxim is the one that my teacher Muhammad Ali ibn Abd al-Wadud, may God have mercy on him, put into verse when he said:

[The four lines of verse are printed in the source with their hemistichs mis-paired; each line is set out as first hemistich, three asterisks, second hemistich, as follows:]

*Naming an entity by other than its name *** it entails no prohibition, nor does it entail*

*rather its ruling formerly, in its yesterday *** an important point, which ought*

*Entities are not transferred from their ruling *** the establishing of a right that is not in its allotment*

*as their ruling afterwards, in its today *** to halt whoever gives a fatwa upon understanding it*

[Read with the hemistichs paired as sense and rhyme require, the four lines run: *Naming an entity by other than its name does not transfer entities from their ruling; rather their ruling formerly, in their yesterday, is as their ruling afterwards, in their today. It entails no prohibition, nor does it entail the establishing of a right that is not in its allotment. An important point, which ought to halt whoever gives a fatwa upon understanding it.*]

Likewise, these photographic images cannot be brought by analogy (qiyās) under the real images concerning which the texts came down, because the operative cause (ʿillah) is different. The operative cause for which the Prophet, may God bless him and grant him peace, forbade image-making, he himself made clear: that it is a vying with God's creation and an imitation of it. That is why the image-maker is punished on the Day of Resurrection: whoever made an image of a thing possessing a soul is punished until he breathes a soul into it, and he will not be one who breathes. And that is why he said: "Those who vie with My creation — let them create an ant, let them create a grain of barley." So he made clear the operative cause of the prohibition.

This operative cause is not realised in photographic images. For that reason, no one can be praised for being a better image-maker than another; he may be praised for being more skilled and more knowledgeable in the use of the apparatus, for instance, or more precise in adjusting it — and that is not image-making itself.

For this reason, as regards photographic images: when the thing photographed is something it is lawful to look at, it is permissible to produce them. The evidence for that is that the basic ruling in all things is permissibility (ibāḥah), and that the capturing — the capturing of the shadow — is in the position of looking into a mirror; and it is established that the Prophet, may God bless him and grant him peace, used to look into the mirror.

The ruling on looking at images and on owning them

The question: What is the ruling on looking at images and on owning them — for example a picture of a brother, or a husband, or a friend?

The answer: If that is by photographic imaging, and not by pictorial imaging, that is, by drawing, then there is no harm in looking at it, so long as it does not contain nakedness (ʿawrah) that it is not lawful to look at. For everything that it is permissible to look at, it is permissible to photograph by photographic imaging.

flags.arabic: تسمية العين بغير اسمها *** لا تقتضي منعاً ولا تقتضي / بل حكمها من قبل في أمسها *** فائدة مهمة ينبغي / لا تنقل الأعيان عن حكمها *** إثبات حق ليس في قسمها / كحكمها من بعد في يومها *** إيقاف من يفتي على فهمها
flags.context: the four lines of nazm by the Sheikh's teacher Muhammad Ali ibn Abd al-Wadud
options: print the lines as the source pairs them AND supply the evident pairing, both marked
flags.note:
SOURCE DEFECT (house rule 11), verified in the page's HTML: the four lines are each in their own

in the source, so the mis-pairing is in the published page and is not an artefact of extraction. The source pairs first hemistich 1 with second hemistich 3, first 2 with second 4, and so on — the signature of a two-column Word table flattened row-wise on paste. Paired as the rhyme (-mihā) and the sense require, the lines read: (1) naming an entity by other than its name / does not transfer entities from their ruling; (2) rather their ruling formerly, in their yesterday / is as their ruling afterwards, in their today; (3) it entails no prohibition / nor the establishing of a right that is not in its allotment; (4) an important point, which ought / to halt whoever gives a fatwa upon understanding it. Both the printed order and the evident order are given in body_en, each marked; body_ar preserves the source exactly. Not silently repaired. This verse is the hinge of the whole fatwa — it is the maxim the ruling rests on — so leaving it as nonsense would gut the argument. Rendered as prose in italics per style guide section 4; no rhymed English attempted.

flags.context: alternative names people give to photography
options: some people call it ṣanf (sense uncertain; left untranslated)
flags.note: UNRESOLVED. الصنف in standard Arabic means a kind, sort or category, which makes no sense as a name for photography beside التمثيل ('depiction'), which the same sentence gives. It may be a Mauritanian or Shinqiti usage, or a source corruption. Left transliterated and untranslated rather than guessed, per style guide section 5. Needs the Sheikh's office.

flags.arabic: "إن قوماً في آخر الزمان يستحلون الخمر يسمونها بغير اسمها" … "المضاهون خلقي فليخلقوا ذرة فليخلقوا شعيرة"
flags.context: the two prophetic reports quoted in the answer
options: reproduce each report with no collection, narrator or grading, as the source does
supply the standard references and wordings
flags.note: Both reports are quoted from memory, with no narrator, no collection and no grading, and both differ from the best-known wordings (the second is ordinarily 'and who does greater wrong than one who goes to create as I create? Let them create an ant, or let them create a grain, or let them create a grain of barley'). Style guide section 4 forbids adding a grading or an attribution the Sheikh did not give, and house rule 11 forbids restoring quoted scripture from memory, so neither has been done. The variation is recorded here instead.

flags.context: the illustration of interpreting the Qur'an by a later sense of a word
options: And there came a caravan, and they sent their water-drawer
And a travelling party came, and they sent their water-carrier
flags.note: Sūrat Yūsuf 12:19. The whole point of the illustration is that sayyārah meant a travelling company and now means a motor car, so the English must use a word that cannot be read as 'car'; 'caravan' does that, and the Arabic word is then named explicitly in the next clause so that the joke about the Caprice and the Land Rover lands. Qur'anic renderings in this corpus are interpretive and are not a substitute for the Arabic.

flags.context: the two examples of modern motor cars
options: a Caprice or a Land Rover
a Capris or a Land Rover
flags.note: كابرس is the Chevrolet Caprice, long a common car in the Gulf and West Africa. The reading is near-certain but is recorded because it rests on regional familiarity rather than on the Arabic.

flags.arabic: وأن الحبس حبس الظل هو بمثابة النظر في المرآة
flags.context: the evidence for permissibility at the end of the first answer
options: that the capturing — the capturing of the shadow — is in the position of looking into a mirror
that the capturing of the shadow is in the position of looking into a mirror
flags.note: SOURCE DEFECT (house rule 11), minor: الحبس حبس الظل is a dittography, almost certainly of speech transcribed. The repetition is kept visible in the English rather than tidied away, and body_ar preserves it.

flags.arabic: ومن فسر الألفاظ الواردة في التصوير بها … وهو من القول على الله بغير علم
flags.context: the Sheikh's characterisation of the contrary position
options: keep the force of the Arabic: contrary to the purpose of the Sharia, and speaking about God without knowledge
soften to 'departs from the intent of the Sharia'
flags.note: The Sheikh is characterising the position of scholars who hold photography forbidden, and the characterisation is severe. Style guide section 6 forbids softening it, and it has not been softened. Recorded so that a reviewer sees the choice was deliberate.

flags.context: the CMS timestamp on the record
options: treat as the date the item was uploaded to the CMS
treat as the date of composition
flags.note: CORPUS-WIDE DEFECT. The CMS serves a bulk-upload timestamp, not the date the Sheikh spoke or wrote. date_is_cms_upload is set true. Where the body itself names a date, that internal date is the better evidence and is kept in the English.

translator_notes: Two distinct fatwas in one record: the main one on producing photographs, and a short second one under its own heading on looking at photographs and keeping them. The site runs them together with no separator other than the heading; the English keeps the heading.

التصوير is rendered 'image-making' throughout rather than 'photography', because the entire argument turns on the claim that the word of the prophetic texts does not reach the modern referent. Where the text means photography specifically it says الصور الفوتوغرافية, rendered 'photographic images'.
يجوز عملها is rendered 'it is permissible to produce them'; jāʾiz here is the legal sense, an act, not the kalām modality of addendum section 8.

حبس الظل, 'the capturing (literally the imprisoning) of the shadow', is the classical Arabic coinage for photography and is kept literal, since the fatwa depends on the fact that the name is a human convention.
The opening question refers to a book called Tafsīr Āyāt al-Aḥkām without naming its author; several works carry that title and none has been identified in the English.
عورة is rendered 'nakedness (ʿawrah)'; it is not in the glossary and the English is the conventional rendering, though the term's extent is itself a matter of juristic disagreement.
